standard.title: Estimation
standard.description: estimate the quantity of objects in collections and make estimates when solving problems to determine the reasonableness of calculations
standard.prior_knowledge: No direct predecessor in progression map. Students have worked with counting and place value but have not yet developed explicit estimation strategies or used estimation to check reasonableness of calculations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students estimate the quantity of objects in collections and use estimation to judge whether calculated answers are reasonable.

nodes.label: Estimation strategies for collections
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can estimate the quantity of objects in a collection using a benchmark or grouping strategy, and explain their reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Estimate the quantity in one collection of 20–100 objects using a stated strategy (chunking or benchmark); compare estimate to actual count.
nodes.typical_width: Estimate quantities across collections of varying sizes using chunking, anchoring and benchmarking strategies; reflect on accuracy of estimates.
wider: Estimate quantities in real-world contexts — number of seeds in a fruit, tiles on a floor, students in an assembly — and discuss sources of estimation error
Explore estimation contexts used in First Nations Australian land management practices (e.g. estimating quantities of food resources)

response_modes.reason: Students need a small repertoire of strategies (chunking, anchoring, benchmarking) to make estimation portable across contexts. Teaching one strategy and moving on limits applicability.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Real-world estimation contexts provide genuine richness — students encounter that estimation is contextually purposeful (when is close enough good enough?) and that different contexts call for different tolerances.
success_criteria: Students can estimate the size of a collection and name the strategy they used.
Students can compare their estimate to the actual count and reflect on its reasonableness.

nodes.label: Estimation to check reasonableness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can estimate the answer to an addition or subtraction problem before calculating, and use the estimate to judge whether their calculated answer is reasonable.
nodes.minimum_width: For two calculation problems, make a prior estimate and then check whether the calculated answer is in the right range; explain the judgment.
nodes.typical_width: Apply estimation to check reasonableness of addition, subtraction and simple multiplication calculations; explain how to recognise an unreasonable answer.
wider: Apply estimation-before-calculation as a regular habit across multiplicative problems, discussing when estimation is more efficient than exact calculation
Investigate how rounding strategies affect estimation accuracy — comparing rounding to nearest 10 vs nearest 100

response_modes.reason: The reasoning chain 'estimate first → calculate → compare → judge' needs explicit scaffolding. Without it, students often treat estimation as an add-on rather than a checking tool.

success_criteria: Students can make a prior estimate for a calculation problem and state a reasonable range.
Students can identify a calculated answer as reasonable or unreasonable based on their estimate and explain why.
